issue.issue_text: Whether the courts below were justified in convicting the petitioners under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 for dishonour of cheques and sentencing them to six months of simple imprisonment and to pay the cheque amounts as compensation.

facts: The petitioners issued five cheques to the complainant to discharge a total liability of Rs. 42,08,000.
All five cheques were dishonoured upon presentation due to 'insufficient funds'.
The petitioners' defence was that the money was not a loan but an investment from the complainant for a joint film production that ultimately failed, and the cheques were subsequently misused.
The petitioners also argued that the complainant failed to prove the source of the funds by not producing account statements or Income Tax Returns.
The Trial Court, the First Appellate Court, and the High Court all found the petitioners guilty under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
law: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, there is a statutory presumption that a cheque was issued for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability.
The onus is on the accused (the person who issued the cheque) to rebut this presumption by raising a probable defence.
This defence must be supported by evidence, either oral or documentary. Merely stating a counter-narrative is not sufficient to shift the burden back to the complainant.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the petitioners admitted to issuing the cheques, which activated the statutory presumption under Section 139.

The Court found that the petitioners failed to provide any evidence to support their claim that the money was an investment for a joint film venture. They did not buttress their defence with any proof.

The Court considered the petitioners' defence to be illogical, questioning why they would issue cheques for repayment (including interest) if the money was an investment in a joint project. This inconsistency was not explained by the petitioners.

Regarding the complainant's failure to produce ITRs, the Court held that this was not fatal to the case. Since the petitioners admitted to receiving the money and did not provide evidence that the complainant lacked the capacity to lend it, the primary burden remained on them to disprove the existence of a legally enforceable debt.
The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to dislodge the statutory presumption that the cheques were issued to repay a legally enforceable debt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the lower courts' decisions, holding that the conviction was justified because the petitioners failed to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act with any credible evidence. However, the Court exercised its judicial discretion to modify the sentence, ordering that the six-month imprisonment terms for each of the five complaints would run concurrently.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the courts below were justified in convicting the petitioners under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 for dishonour of cheques and sentencing them to six months of simple imprisonment and to pay the cheque amounts as compensation.
appellant_arguments: The complainant failed to prove that the cheques were issued for a legally enforceable debt, as no statement of accounts or Income Tax Returns were produced to show a loan was made.
The money was not a loan but an investment for a film being jointly produced by the complainant and the accused.
The cheques and receipts were misused by the complainant after the jointly produced film failed.
The accused rebutted the statutory presumption under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act by establishing a probable defence through cross-examination.
Once the presumption was rebutted, the burden shifted back to the complainant to prove the existence of a legally enforceable debt, which they failed to do.
respondent_arguments: The petitioners' defence that the money was for a film production is merely a counter-stand and is not supported by any oral or documentary evidence.
The petitioners have not denied issuing and signing the cheques, which is a crucial admission.

The complainant's failure to produce a statement of accounts or tax returns is not fatal to the case, especially since the petitioners did not prove the complainant lacked the financial capacity to provide the loan.
If the money was an investment in a joint film venture, there would have been no reason for the petitioners to issue cheques, especially with interest, to the complainant.
The onus remained on the petitioners to prove their defence, and they failed to dislodge the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Act.

cases.principle: Concurrent findings of fact are ordinarily not interfered with by the Supreme Court under its special jurisdiction (Article 136), which is meant mainly to correct manifest injustice or errors of law.

cases.case_name: Kundan Lal Rallaram v. Custodian (Evacuee Property)
cases.principle: A presumption of fact under Section 114 of the Evidence Act can be raised against a party who fails to produce evidence (like account books), and this analogy can be extended to rebut the statutory presumptions under the Negotiable Instruments Act.
Once both parties have adduced evidence, the burden of proof loses its importance, and the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act does not again come to the complainant’s rescue.
Once both parties have adduced evidence, the Court has to consider the same and the burden of proof loses all its importance.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, once the drawer's signature on a cheque is admitted, the court must presume that the cheque was issued for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. This presumption is triggered even if the accused contends that a signed blank cheque was handed over. The burden then shifts to the accused to rebut this presumption by adducing evidence, as merely stating a probable defense or a counter-stand is insufficient to shift the onus back to the complainant.
obiter: Concurrent findings of fact ordinarily acquire a deterrent sanctity and tentative finality when challenged in this Court and we rarely invoke the special jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution which is meant mainly to correct manifest injustice or errors of law of great moment.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The petitioners failed to rebut the statutory presumption that the cheques were issued for a legally enforceable debt because their defense—that the money was for a film production—was merely a counter-stand unsupported by any evidence. The Court found that simply raising a probable defense without adducing evidence is insufficient to shift the onus back onto the complainant.
legal_tests_applied: The Court will necessarily presume that the cheque had been issued towards discharge of a legally enforceable debt/liability in two circumstances. Firstly, when the drawer of the cheque admits issuance/execution of the cheque.
The standard for rebutting the statutory presumption is that the accused must establish a probable defence, after which the presumption is in peril.

The Supreme Court's special jurisdiction under Article 136 is rarely invoked to challenge concurrent findings of fact, as it is meant mainly to correct manifest injustice or errors of law of great moment.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioners failed to adduce any evidence to support their contention that the amounts were given for producing a film and not as a loan.
The Court held that, "Just by taking a counter-stand to raise a probable defence would not shift the onus on the complainant in such cases."
why_respondent_won: The petitioners did not deny issuing the cheques, which triggered the statutory presumption that they were for a legally enforceable debt.

The petitioners failed to adduce any evidence to support their defense, meaning the statutory presumption was never successfully rebutted. The Court found the reasoning of the High Court, First Appellate Court, and Trial Court on this issue to be "sound."
policy_considerations: Concurrent findings of fact ordinarily acquire a deterrent sanctity and tentative finality when challenged in this Court and we rarely invoke the special jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution which is meant mainly to correct manifest injustice or errors of law of great moment.
In directing the sentences to run concurrently, we have exercised judicial discretion.
